referents.why: 'We are slanderously charged' (first plural): Paul and his company; no first-plural candidate.
'Some' (masculine plural) who affirm the slander; the slanderers are not among the candidates (condemnation only).
'Us' is the accusative subject of the infinitive 'to say': the people slandered, Paul and his company; no first-plural candidate. The builder's 'some' is wrong.
'Let us do' (first plural) in the quoted slogan is the group slandered; no candidate. The builder's 'some' is wrong.
'Their' condemnation (masculine plural) refers to the slanderers; no masculine plural candidate, and the only candidate is the condemnation itself.

links.why: Hina: 'let us do evil so that good may come'; the good is the purpose of the evil.
Ruling R1: a saying clause introduces what is said, linked as content, not as that.
'To say' introduces the slogan 'let us do evil that good may come'.
The infinitive 'us to say' is the object of 'affirm'.
'Affirm' introduces the claim that they say this; nested speech gets its own content link (R1).
'Their condemnation is deserved' is the writer's own verdict, not nested in the slanderers' claim.
A clause cannot be joined to itself.
Kai joins the two comparisons: 'we are slanderously charged, and as some affirm'.

groups.why: The claim is the speech of the slanderers, and the inner turn is its part. Cl5 is the writer's own verdict and is removed from the turn. The slanderers are not a candidate, so no sender is given.
The claimed speech 'us to say' has the slogan as its part (ruling R1, nested speech).

none_fit.what: The writer's verdict on the slanderers, not a link to any clause; no link type records a verdict.

cant_tell.what: the sender of the claim in turn0
cant_tell.why: the slanderers ('some') are not offered as candidates
